definition: Mores means the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mores. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mores should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Nothing in the dorm handbook covers it, but hall mores are strict: you do not run the blender during quiet hours, and you replace what you borrow.
Customs are the milder rung — what people usually do, like cake on birthdays; skipping a custom makes you odd, while breaking mores marks a failure of decency.
Laws go further than mores: a law is written down and enforced by courts, while mores are enforced only by a community's regard — though losing that can hurt worse than a fine.

Folkways are the small everyday habits of a people — greetings, table rhythms, which nights the market runs — and they are lightly held. Mores carry moral charge: neglecting a folkway makes you unusual, while breaking mores makes the town doubt your decency.

Norms are all of a group's shared expectations, from dress codes to how a line forms, whatever their weight. Mores are the narrower, heavier set — the norms a community treats as matters of right and wrong, enforced by moral judgment rather than raised eyebrows.

Mores means the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group.

In the county where my father grew up, mores govern a funeral more firmly than any statute: neighbors mow the family's lawn without asking, casseroles arrive unsigned, and nobody sells the bereaved anything for a month.
No council passed these rules and no court could enforce them.
Breaking one simply tells the town, permanently, what you are.
Mores is the precise term because these are the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group — heavier than manners, which merely smooth social traffic.
Skipping the casserole is not impolite; it is felt as a small failure of decency.
That moral charge, enforced by regard rather than law, is what the word names.
Mores is the sociologist's word — always plural, pronounced MOR-ayz — for the customs a group treats as matters of decency.
Etiquette governs forks; mores govern what neighbors owe each other.

Within this unit, keep the lanes: mores are what a community's conscience requires, ritualized describes the fixed form a practice has hardened into, and quotidian describes the everyday texture of what recurs.

mores: Laws go further than mores: a law is written down and enforced by courts, while mores are enforced only by a community's regard — though losing that can hurt worse than a fine.
Aboard a nineteenth-century whaling ship, almost nothing was written down, yet the crew's mores governed the voyage more tightly than the owner's contract did.
A sailor who shirked a watch was mocked; that was a lapse of habit.
But a sailor who stole from a shipmate's sea chest had done something worse in the crew's eyes.
Thieves were not merely teased.
Men refused to eat beside them, and at the next port they often found no ship willing to sign them on.
Historians note that no law required any of this.
The punishment ran on shared moral judgment, passed from forecastle to forecastle.
The code answered a real need: months at sea left no room for a man the others could not trust.
